name: The Security Citadel
description: Network security — attacks, defences, encryption, VPNs, and access control.

nodes.name: The Threat Landscape
nodes.description: Attack types, social engineering, DDoS categories, and threat actors.

encounters.title: The Unwanted House Guests: A Malware Taxonomy
encounters.scenario: Malware = unwanted house guests. A VIRUS can't get in alone — YOU must run an infected file/macro — then it attaches to other files and spreads only when those are shared. A WORM picks the lock itself and self-propagates across the network with zero user action. A TROJAN shows up disguised as something desirable ('free software') so you let it in voluntarily, but it's not what it claims. A ROOTKIT doesn't just get in — it hides inside the walls at OS/kernel level, invisible to normal security tools. KEYLOGGER/SPYWARE silently photocopies everything you type, including passwords. A LOGIC BOMB plants a hidden device that does nothing until a specific date or condition triggers it.
encounters.question: An employee opens an email attachment disguised as an invoice. Nothing visibly happens, but weeks later, security analysts discover the program has been embedded in the OS kernel, hiding its own process from Task Manager and antivirus scans, while a separate hidden routine is set to wipe the file server on the date the employee's manager is scheduled to leave the company. Which TWO malware characteristics are present in this scenario?
options: A worm (self-propagating across the network) and a virus (requires a host file to spread)
A trojan (disguised as a legitimate file to gain initial entry) combined with a rootkit (kernel-level hiding) and a logic bomb (triggers on a future condition)
Ransomware (encrypts files for payment) and spyware (logs keystrokes)
A logic bomb only — the disguised attachment and kernel hiding are both side effects of the same logic bomb mechanism
encounters.explanation: The disguised attachment = TROJAN (looks legitimate to gain entry). Hiding from Task Manager/AV at kernel level = ROOTKIT. The routine triggered by a future date = LOGIC BOMB. Wrong: (A) nothing here self-propagates to other hosts or attaches to files to spread, ruling out worm/virus. (C) no files are encrypted for ransom, and the kernel-hiding plus timed wipe described isn't keystroke logging, ruling out ransomware/spyware. (D) a logic bomb is just the trigger — it doesn't explain HOW the malware got in (trojan) or stayed hidden (rootkit); these are three separate techniques working together.

encounters.title: Who's Casing the Building? Profiling Threat Actors
encounters.scenario: Different people 'casing' a building reveal different threat actors. A SCRIPT KIDDIE is a teenager rattling door handles with a borrowed crowbar — low skill, using downloaded tools they barely understand, often just to see what happens. A HACKTIVIST spray-paints a slogan in broad daylight — the goal is the MESSAGE and VISIBILITY (defacement, leaked documents, a DDoS with a press release), not staying hidden. ORGANISED CRIME is a professional burglary crew — methodical and financially motivated, after something sellable (data, ransomware payouts, fraud). An INSIDER THREAT already has a key — a current/former employee misusing legitimate access, which is why they're hard to detect. An ADVANCED PERSISTENT THREAT (often nation-state) doesn't break in loudly — it rents the apartment next door for years, tunnelling through slowly, prioritizing long-term undetected access over a quick score.
encounters.question: A forensic investigation traces a breach to a phishing email opened 14 months ago by an employee in the accounts department. Since that initial access, an external attacker has maintained undetected access to the file server, exfiltrating small amounts of data during normal business hours specifically to blend in with regular traffic, with no public statement or visible disruption at any point. Which threat actor category does this MOST likely describe?
options: Script kiddie — using a phishing email is the hallmark of a low-skill, off-the-shelf attack
Hacktivist — the long-term campaign shows a clear ideological commitment
Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) — the long dwell time, stealth, and low-and-slow exfiltration designed to blend in are the defining characteristics
Insider threat — only someone with existing employee credentials could access the file server for 14 months
encounters.explanation: APT's name says it all: ADVANCED (evaded detection over a year by mimicking normal traffic), PERSISTENT (14 months of access), THREAT (ongoing exfiltration). Wrong: (A) script kiddies are noisy and short-lived — sustaining 14+ months of stealth takes far more discipline than 'borrowed tools.' (B) hacktivism is defined by visibility (manifesto, defacement, public DDoS); the scenario explicitly says there was none. (D) the initial access came via an EXTERNAL attacker phishing the employee — the employee was a victim, not the perpetrator; an outsider patiently operating for a year is the textbook APT pattern.

encounters.question: An attacker sends thousands of SYN packets to a server without completing the TCP handshake. What attack is this?
options: UDP flood
SYN flood (DoS — protocol attack)
DNS amplification
Ping of Death
encounters.explanation: SYN flood: attacker sends SYN but never completes the 3-way handshake. The server allocates state for each half-open connection until its table fills — legitimate connections are refused. Mitigation: SYN cookies (server doesn't allocate state until handshake complete).

encounters.question: Phishing, spear phishing, and whaling are all forms of which broader attack category?
options: DDoS
Social engineering
Physical intrusion
On-path attacks
encounters.explanation: All three are social engineering — manipulating humans to divulge information or perform actions. Phishing = mass/generic. Spear phishing = targeted. Whaling = specifically targets senior executives (C-suite).

encounters.question: An attacker sends fraudulent ARP replies to associate their MAC address with the gateway IP. What attack is this?
options: DNS poisoning
ARP poisoning
DHCP starvation
IP spoofing
encounters.explanation: ARP poisoning (ARP spoofing): the attacker poisons ARP caches — hosts send traffic destined for the gateway to the attacker instead, enabling man-in-the-middle interception. Mitigation: Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) on switches.

encounters.question: Vishing is a social engineering attack conducted via:
options: Email
SMS text message
Voice call or phone
Physical impersonation in person
encounters.explanation: Vishing = Voice Phishing. Attacker calls the victim impersonating IT support, a bank, government agency, etc. Smishing = SMS. Phishing = email. All exploit trust and urgency.

encounters.question: A DDoS attack differs from a DoS attack primarily because:
options: DDoS only targets web servers
DDoS uses a distributed botnet of many compromised hosts — harder to block a single source
DDoS operates at Layer 7 only
DoS attacks are more damaging
encounters.explanation: DoS = single source. DDoS = Distributed — botnet of thousands of compromised machines launch the attack simultaneously. DDoS is much harder to mitigate because you can't block a single source IP.

encounters.question: An attacker sets up a Wi-Fi network with the same SSID as the corporate network to trick users into connecting. This is called:
options: Rogue DHCP server
Evil twin AP
War driving
Deauth attack
encounters.explanation: Evil twin: a fake AP broadcasting the same SSID as the legitimate network. Users connect thinking it's real — attacker intercepts all traffic. Mitigation: 802.1X Enterprise authentication (rogue AP cannot present valid RADIUS credentials).

encounters.question: Password spraying differs from brute force in that password spraying:
options: Tries all possible passwords against one account
Tries a few common passwords across many accounts — avoids triggering lockout policies
Uses pre-computed hash tables
Only targets admin accounts
encounters.explanation: Password spraying: try 'Password1', 'Spring2024', 'CompanyName1' against thousands of accounts — stays under lockout threshold per account. Brute force: try every possible password against one account — quickly triggers lockout. Spray = stealth; brute = loud.

encounters.question: DNS poisoning attacks work by:
options: Overloading DNS servers with requests
Injecting forged DNS records into a resolver's cache to redirect users to malicious sites
Brute-forcing DNS zone transfer credentials
Intercepting HTTPS traffic to DNS servers
encounters.explanation: DNS cache poisoning: attacker injects forged DNS responses into a recursive resolver's cache. Users querying that resolver get malicious IPs for legitimate domains — redirected without knowing. Mitigation: DNSSEC (cryptographically signs DNS records).

encounters.question: An on-path attack (formerly MITM) positions the attacker between two communicating hosts. Which technology BEST prevents this on encrypted connections?
options: Firewall ACLs
Certificate validation + mutual TLS authentication
Port security on switches
VLAN segmentation
encounters.explanation: TLS with proper certificate validation prevents MITM — the client verifies the server's certificate is signed by a trusted CA and matches the intended hostname. Mutual TLS (client + server certificates) provides bi-directional authentication. An attacker cannot forge a valid certificate.

encounters.question: A rogue DHCP server attack can be mitigated by which switch feature?
options: Port security
DHCP snooping
Dynamic ARP Inspection
Storm control
encounters.explanation: DHCP snooping designates switch ports as trusted (uplink to real DHCP server) or untrusted (client ports). DHCP OFFER and ACK messages on untrusted ports are dropped — preventing rogue DHCP servers from distributing malicious gateway/DNS settings.

encounters.question: Which attack uses pre-computed hash tables to crack password hashes, and what defeats it?
options: Brute force — defeated by complexity requirements
Rainbow table attack — defeated by salting password hashes before storage
SYN flood — defeated by SYN cookies
Dictionary attack — defeated by lockout policies
encounters.explanation: Rainbow tables are pre-computed plaintext→hash mappings. An attacker with a stolen password hash database can look up hashes to find passwords instantly. Salting adds a unique random value to each password before hashing — same password produces different hashes, defeating pre-computed tables.

encounters.question: An employee receives a text message claiming their package is delayed and asks them to click a link to reschedule. This is:
options: Phishing
Vishing
Smishing
Pretexting
encounters.explanation: Smishing = SMS phishing. Text messages (SMS) used to deliver a malicious link or extract information. The package delivery pretense is a common smishing lure. Vishing = voice call. Phishing = email.

encounters.question: A DNS amplification attack is a volumetric DDoS technique. How does the amplification work?
options: Attacker directly sends massive DNS queries to the victim
Attacker sends small DNS queries with the victim's spoofed IP as source — open resolvers send large responses to the victim
Attacker poisons DNS cache to redirect victims to malicious IPs
Attacker intercepts DNS responses and replaces them with malicious entries
encounters.explanation: DNS amplification: attacker spoofs victim's IP and sends small DNS queries (requesting large record types like ANY or TXT) to open recursive resolvers. Resolvers send large responses to the victim's IP. Amplification factor can be 50x — small query creates large attack traffic aimed at victim.

encounters.question: A deauthentication attack against wireless clients is best mitigated by:
options: WPA2 PSK with a strong passphrase
802.11w (Management Frame Protection) and WPA3
Disabling SSID broadcasting
Using channels 1, 6, or 11
encounters.explanation: Deauth attacks send spoofed management frames (deauthentication) to force clients off the AP — enabling MITM or forcing WPA2 handshake capture. 802.11w (MFP) adds cryptographic protection to management frames, preventing spoofing. WPA3 also requires MFP.

encounters.question: Tailgating (piggybacking) is a physical security attack where:
options: An attacker monitors network traffic from a nearby location
An attacker follows an authorised person through a secured door without using their own credentials
An attacker installs a keylogger on a target's computer
An attacker uses social media to gather target information
encounters.explanation: Tailgating: attacker physically follows an authorised employee through badge-access doors — exploiting courtesy (holding the door). Mitigations: mantraps/airlocks (only one person per cycle), security awareness training, security guards.

encounters.question: An APT (Advanced Persistent Threat) is distinguished from other attacks by:
options: Using only volumetric DDoS techniques
Long-term, stealthy access — often nation-state sponsored — focused on espionage rather than immediate disruption
Targeting only financial institutions
Requiring physical access to the target
encounters.explanation: APT = long-term, stealthy, targeted. Nation-state actors often run APTs to maintain persistent access for intelligence gathering — staying hidden for months or years. Contrast with script kiddies (noisy, opportunistic) or ransomware gangs (quick financial payoff).

nodes.name: The Perimeter Wall
nodes.description: Firewalls, IDS/IPS, DMZ, network segmentation, and Zero Trust architecture.

encounters.title: Badge at the Door vs Badge at Every Door: Zero Trust
encounters.scenario: A traditional office has ONE checkpoint at the front door — badge in once, then walk to any floor, office, or cabinet with no further checks. This is PERIMETER-BASED security: a strong wall around a 'trusted' inside and an 'untrusted' outside. The flaw: if an employee's badge is stolen (or their laptop is phished), the attacker is INSIDE with full freedom of movement and nothing else will catch them. ZERO TRUST flips this: now EVERY door — every office, cabinet, server room — has its OWN badge reader, regardless of whether you already badged in at the front. Every access request is independently authenticated and authorized: 'never trust, always verify.' A stolen badge still gets past the front door, but it won't open the server room or finance database — those check credentials again, every time.
encounters.question: An employee's laptop is compromised via a phishing email while connected to the internal corporate Wi-Fi. In a traditional PERIMETER-based security model, what is the most significant immediate risk — and how would a Zero Trust architecture change that outcome?
options: Traditional: the firewall would have already blocked the phishing email, so this scenario couldn't happen under either model.

Traditional: because the laptop is already 'inside' the trusted network, the attacker likely has broad lateral access to internal resources with no further checks; Zero Trust requires every resource access to be re-authenticated and authorized regardless of network location, sharply limiting lateral movement.
Traditional and Zero Trust behave identically once a device is connected to the internal network — the security model only affects external/remote connections.
Zero Trust would have prevented the phishing email from being delivered in the first place, since it inspects all inbound email content.
encounters.explanation: This is Zero Trust's core motivation: in a perimeter model, 'inside the network' is treated as trustworthy, so one compromised device can move laterally with little friction. Zero Trust removes that assumption — every resource access requires its own check, containing the blast radius to only what that session was explicitly granted. Wrong: (A) phishing routinely bypasses filters — that's why this scenario is common. (C) Zero Trust applies scrutiny INSIDE the network too, the opposite of perimeter models. (D) Zero Trust governs resource access, not email filtering — it doesn't claim to stop phishing delivery.

encounters.title: The Broken Turnstile: Fail-Open vs Fail-Closed
encounters.scenario: A subway turnstile breaks two possible ways. FAIL-OPEN: the arm springs open and stays open — everyone walks through freely, ticket or not. Commuters keep moving (availability preserved), but ticket-checking has stopped (security is gone) until it's fixed. FAIL-CLOSED: the arm locks rigidly — NOBODY gets through, valid ticket or not, until repaired. Security is preserved, but availability is completely lost. An inline IPS sits directly in the traffic path, like that turnstile — and when it crashes or loses power, it must be built (often via a hardware bypass/TAP) to do ONE of these two things. Neither is universally 'correct'; it's a deliberate availability-vs-security tradeoff.
encounters.question: A company deploys an inline IPS between its core switch and edge router. During a software update, the IPS crashes unexpectedly. Network monitoring shows that traffic continued flowing between the LAN and the internet throughout the crash, completely uninspected, until the IPS came back online 10 minutes later. Which failure mode was this IPS configured for, and what is the security implication?
options: Fail-closed — all traffic was blocked until the IPS recovered, which is why the outage lasted 10 minutes.

Fail-open — traffic passed through uninspected during the outage, prioritizing availability over security; this represents a real (if temporary) security gap with zero intrusion detection/prevention active.
Active-active clustering — the IPS automatically failed over to a redundant unit with no service interruption or security gap.
This is impossible — an inline device that crashes must always stop all traffic through it, regardless of configuration.
encounters.explanation: Traffic 'continued flowing... completely uninspected' during the crash — that's the definition of fail-open. The 10-minute window is a real security gap: no IPS signatures were checked, so attack traffic would have passed freely. Wrong: (A) fail-CLOSED means total connectivity loss during the crash, the opposite of what's described. (C) nothing indicates a redundant unit or automatic failover — 'uninspected' rules out a seamless handoff to a working IPS. (D) this is exactly why fail-open hardware bypass exists — many inline appliances include a physical bypass (relay/optical switch) that connects the wire pairs directly when the inspection engine fails, keeping the link up.

encounters.question: The key difference between a stateless and stateful firewall is:
options: Stateless firewalls are faster but inspect application payloads
Stateful firewalls track connection state — return traffic is automatically permitted without explicit rules
Stateless firewalls only work at Layer 7
Stateful firewalls cannot filter by port number
encounters.explanation: Stateful firewalls maintain a connection state table. When an internal host initiates a TCP connection outbound, the returning traffic is automatically allowed because the firewall recognizes it belongs to an established session. Stateless firewalls evaluate every packet independently — you need explicit rules for return traffic.

encounters.question: IDS differs from IPS in that IDS:
options: Blocks malicious traffic inline
Detects and alerts only — does NOT block traffic
Is always host-based
Requires a RADIUS server
encounters.explanation: IDS (Intrusion Detection System) = passive — monitors traffic and generates alerts. It does NOT block. IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) = active/inline — sits in the traffic path and can DROP malicious traffic in real time.

encounters.question: A DMZ (Demilitarized Zone) is used to:
options: Isolate management traffic from user traffic
Place public-facing servers between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network
Create a separate VLAN for guest users
Encrypt traffic between branch offices
encounters.explanation: The DMZ (screened subnet) is a buffer zone for public-facing services — web, email, DNS. Internet users can reach DMZ servers, but DMZ servers cannot initiate connections to the internal LAN. If a DMZ server is compromised, the attacker is still blocked from the internal network.

encounters.question: A WAF (Web Application Firewall) is specifically designed to protect against:
options: Network-layer DDoS attacks
Web application attacks such as SQL injection, XSS, and CSRF (OWASP Top 10)
Brute force against SSH services
BGP hijacking at the routing layer
encounters.explanation: WAF specifically inspects HTTP/HTTPS traffic for web application attacks — SQL injection, cross-site scripting (XSS), CSRF, path traversal, etc. (OWASP Top 10). A standard firewall cannot detect these attacks because they are hidden within legitimate HTTP requests.

encounters.question: A honeypot in network security is:
options: An encrypted password vault for storing credentials
A decoy system designed to attract attackers and log their techniques
A backup DNS server
A type of IPS signature database
encounters.explanation: A honeypot is a fake, deliberately vulnerable system with no legitimate traffic. Any access to it is suspicious. It logs attacker techniques, tools, and IPs — providing threat intelligence. A honeynet is a network of multiple honeypots.

encounters.question: Zero Trust security is based on which core principle?
options: Trust all internal traffic; verify external traffic only
Never trust, always verify — every access request requires authentication and authorisation regardless of network location
Trust is granted once per user per session
Only external connections need encryption
encounters.explanation: Zero Trust: no implicit trust based on network location (even being inside the corporate network). Every user, device, and application must authenticate and be authorised for every resource. Microsegmentation and continuous verification are core Zero Trust controls.

encounters.question: Defense in depth means:
options: Placing the firewall deep in the network
Layering multiple overlapping security controls so compromise of one layer doesn't lead to full breach
Using deep packet inspection on all traffic
Encrypting data at multiple OSI layers
encounters.explanation: Defense in depth (castle model): multiple layers of security — perimeter firewall, IPS, network segmentation, endpoint protection, DLP, encryption, MFA, etc. An attacker who bypasses one layer faces the next. No single control is sufficient.

encounters.question: An IPS generates a false positive. What is the impact?
options: A real attack is not detected
Legitimate traffic is blocked — potential service disruption
The IPS stops monitoring
Alerts are sent to the wrong destination
encounters.explanation: A false positive on an IPS means the system incorrectly identifies legitimate traffic as malicious and DROPS it. This can block users, services, or applications. False positives are a key operational challenge with IPS — signatures must be carefully tuned.

encounters.question: A jump server (bastion host) is used for:
options: Routing traffic between DMZ and internal network
Providing a hardened, audited single access point to manage sensitive internal systems remotely
Hosting public web applications in the DMZ
Accelerating encrypted VPN connections
encounters.explanation: A bastion host/jump server is a hardened gateway: admins connect to it first (typically via SSH or RDP), then access internal servers from there. All commands are logged for audit. It reduces the attack surface by limiting direct external access to internal management interfaces.

encounters.question: Microsegmentation in a data centre applies firewall policies at:
options: The perimeter only
Per-workload or per-VM level — controls East-West traffic inside the data centre
Only between DMZ and internal LAN
The ISP edge router
encounters.explanation: Microsegmentation applies granular firewall rules between individual workloads or VMs inside the data centre — controlling East-West (lateral) traffic. Traditional firewalls only control North-South (in/out) traffic. Microsegmentation limits lateral movement if one VM is compromised.

encounters.question: A NGFW identifies application traffic regardless of port number. What capability enables this?
options: Deep packet inspection with App-ID (application identification)
Stateful connection tracking
Certificate revocation checking
MAC address filtering
encounters.explanation: NGFW App-ID uses deep packet inspection, protocol decoders, and behavioral analysis to identify applications regardless of port — e.g., BitTorrent on port 80 is still identified as BitTorrent, not HTTP. This is impossible with traditional port-based firewalls.

encounters.question: A company's web server in the DMZ is compromised. With a proper two-firewall DMZ design, what is the attacker's next obstacle?
options: The compromised web server's local firewall
The inner firewall separating the DMZ from the internal LAN — which blocks DMZ-initiated connections inbound
The ISP's edge router
The RADIUS server
encounters.explanation: Proper DMZ design: outer firewall (internet→DMZ) + inner firewall (DMZ→LAN). The inner firewall blocks unsolicited connections from the DMZ to the LAN. A compromised DMZ server cannot directly reach internal systems — the inner firewall limits blast radius.

encounters.question: UTM (Unified Threat Management) is best described as:
options: A routing protocol for secure networks
A single appliance combining firewall, IPS, antivirus, web filter, VPN, and DLP
A type of honeypot deployment
A wireless security framework
encounters.explanation: UTM consolidates multiple security functions into one device — reducing cost and complexity for small/medium businesses. Downside: single point of failure, potential performance bottleneck, and less flexibility than best-of-breed individual solutions.

encounters.question: The implicit deny rule at the end of every firewall ACL means:
options: Traffic matching the last explicit rule is denied
Any traffic not matched by a permit rule above is automatically dropped
The firewall denies all traffic until a permit rule is added
Only outbound traffic is implicitly denied
encounters.explanation: Implicit deny: the last (invisible) rule at the bottom of every ACL drops ALL traffic not explicitly permitted above. You don't see it, but it's always there. This is why forgetting to add a needed permit rule causes mysterious connectivity issues.

encounters.question: An IDS is deployed in tap/SPAN mode. If it detects a serious attack, what limitation exists?
options: It cannot generate alerts
It cannot block the attack — it can only alert. Traffic has already passed before detection.
It will automatically update firewall rules
It will terminate the attacker's connection directly
encounters.explanation: IDS in tap/SPAN mode receives a copy of traffic — it is out-of-band. By the time it generates an alert, the attack traffic has already been forwarded to the target. IDS can log and alert but CANNOT block. An IPS deployed inline can drop packets before they reach the destination.

nodes.name: The Secret Tunnels
nodes.description: VPN technologies, IPsec modes, SSL/TLS, PKI, and cryptographic concepts.

encounters.title: The Locked Box and the Key Courier: Hybrid Encryption in TLS
encounters.scenario: You need to send a friend a heavy locked strongbox, but you've never met and share no secret. ASYMMETRIC encryption solves the 'never met' problem: your friend mails you their open PADLOCK (public key) — anyone can click it shut, but only their matching private key opens it. The catch: this lock-and-key math is far too slow for an entire strongbox of documents. So you use the padlock to secure a tiny envelope containing a SHARED COMBINATION (a symmetric session key) — one small, slow operation. Once your friend opens that envelope, you BOTH hold the same combination, and every document afterward is locked/unlocked with fast SYMMETRIC encryption (like AES) — thousands of times faster.
encounters.question: A packet capture of a TLS handshake shows the client and server using RSA or ECDHE to agree on a 'pre-master secret,' but the bulk of the session's traffic is encrypted with AES-256-GCM. Why does TLS use TWO different types of encryption instead of just one?
options: AES is considered insecure for key exchange, so RSA must always run first as a security upgrade

Asymmetric encryption (RSA/ECDHE) solves the problem of securely agreeing on a secret with no prior shared key, but it's computationally expensive; once both sides share a symmetric session key, fast AES handles the bulk data — this combination is called hybrid encryption
RSA encrypts the connection metadata while AES encrypts only the TCP headers
The handshake uses AES first to establish the connection, and RSA only encrypts the final few packets for extra protection
encounters.explanation: Asymmetric encryption (RSA/ECDHE) is the only practical way for two parties with no prior shared secret to agree on one, but it's far too slow for bulk data. Symmetric AES is fast but needs a shared key first. TLS combines both: use the slow asymmetric step ONCE to establish a session key, then fast AES for everything else — HYBRID encryption. Wrong: (A) AES isn't 'insecure' for key exchange, it's USELESS for it — symmetric algorithms require the key to already be shared. (C) RSA/ECDHE establishes the session key, not metadata; AES encrypts the whole payload, not just headers. (D) reverses the order — asymmetric happens FIRST, then AES handles the bulk session.

encounters.title: The Notarized Letter vs the Letter You Wrote Yourself: Certificate Trust Chains
encounters.scenario: A digital certificate is a letter of introduction: 'I certify this server really is hr.internal.corp.' The question is always WHO certifies it, and do you already trust THEM? A cert signed by a public CA (DigiCert, Let's Encrypt) is like a letter notarized by a notary your browser already recognizes — its root cert ships pre-installed, so the chain is unbroken. A SELF-SIGNED cert is a letter you wrote and signed yourself — it might say all the right things, but nobody trusts YOUR signature, since no chain leads to a recognized notary. Browsers flag this 'untrusted' not because encryption is broken, but because identity can't be verified. Many ORGANIZATIONS run an INTERNAL CA and push its root cert to managed devices (via Group Policy/MDM) — to those devices, internally-signed certs are fully trusted.
encounters.question: An employee visiting https://hr.internal.corp on their personal laptop gets a 'Your connection is not private (NET::ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID)' warning. A coworker visiting the exact same URL on a company-managed laptop sees no warning at all. What is the MOST likely explanation?
options: The connection is unencrypted on the personal laptop but encrypted on the company laptop

The HR portal uses a certificate signed by the company's internal CA. The managed laptop has that internal CA's root certificate in its trusted store and can build a complete chain; the personal laptop doesn't, so the chain is broken — the connection may still be encrypted, but the identity can't be verified
The certificate has expired, but only according to the personal laptop's clock
This always indicates an active man-in-the-middle attack targeting the personal laptop specifically
encounters.explanation: 'Untrusted CA' means the browser couldn't build a chain back to a root it trusts — it does NOT mean the connection is unencrypted (TLS can succeed even when identity verification fails). The classic cause: a private CA. The managed laptop has the org's internal root pre-installed and validates the chain; the personal laptop never received that root, so the same cert looks 'untrusted.' Wrong: (A) encryption and identity verification are separate checks. (C) clock-skew gives a different error (CERT_DATE_INVALID) and would affect both devices equally. (D) one device erroring while another doesn't, on an internal site, points to a missing root CA, not an active attack.

encounters.question: IPsec ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload) provides:
options: Authentication only — no encryption
Encryption, integrity, and authentication of the payload
Only IP header authentication
NAT traversal capability
encounters.explanation: ESP (IP protocol 50) provides confidentiality (encryption), integrity, and authentication of the payload. AH (IP protocol 51) provides only integrity and authentication — NO encryption. Almost all deployments use ESP.

encounters.question: SSL/TLS VPN has an advantage over IPsec VPN because:
options: It uses stronger encryption
It operates over HTTPS (port 443) — usually not blocked by firewalls; easier for remote users
It is faster than IPsec
It requires no client software
encounters.explanation: SSL/TLS VPN uses port 443 (HTTPS) — rarely blocked because it's the same port used for all web traffic. IPsec uses UDP 500/4500, which can be blocked by strict firewalls. SSL VPN is also available clientless via browser (for portal access).

encounters.question: IPsec Tunnel mode vs Transport mode: which one is used for site-to-site VPNs?
options: Transport mode — encrypts only the payload
Tunnel mode — encrypts the entire original packet and adds a new outer IP header
Both are equivalent for site-to-site
Neither — site-to-site uses GRE only
encounters.explanation: Tunnel mode encrypts the ENTIRE original IP packet (header + payload) and wraps it in a new outer IP header with the VPN gateway addresses. This is required for site-to-site VPNs because the original private IPs need to be hidden and transported across the internet.

encounters.question: AES is classified as which type of encryption algorithm?
options: Asymmetric
Symmetric
Hashing
Elliptic curve
encounters.explanation: AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) is a symmetric block cipher — same key encrypts and decrypts. It is the standard for bulk data encryption (VPN tunnels, disk encryption, TLS session data). RSA and ECC are asymmetric algorithms.

encounters.question: A digital certificate's primary purpose is to:
options: Encrypt all network traffic automatically
Bind a public key to a verified identity, signed by a trusted Certificate Authority
Replace the need for passwords
Enable faster routing between networks
encounters.explanation: A digital certificate (X.509) contains a public key, the identity it belongs to, validity period, and is digitally signed by a CA. Anyone trusting that CA can verify the certificate is authentic — enabling TLS/HTTPS, email signing, VPN authentication.

encounters.question: Split tunneling in a VPN means:
options: Two VPN tunnels run simultaneously for redundancy
Only corporate/private traffic routes through the VPN — internet traffic goes directly via the local ISP
The VPN connection is divided into authentication and data channels
Traffic is split evenly across two VPN gateways
encounters.explanation: Split tunneling: only traffic destined for corporate networks goes through the VPN tunnel. Internet traffic (YouTube, social media) exits locally via the user's ISP. This reduces VPN gateway load but means internet traffic is NOT protected by corporate security controls.

encounters.question: IKE Phase 1 in IPsec negotiation establishes:
options: The actual IPsec data tunnel (ESP/AH parameters)
A secure management channel (ISAKMP SA) used to protect Phase 2 negotiations
The symmetric session key directly
The routing table entries for VPN traffic
encounters.explanation: IKE Phase 1 creates the ISAKMP SA (Security Association) — a secure, authenticated channel between the two VPN endpoints using Diffie-Hellman key exchange. Phase 2 then negotiates the actual IPsec SA (ESP/AH parameters) within this protected channel.

encounters.question: CRL vs OCSP: when checking if a certificate has been revoked, OCSP is preferred because:
options: OCSP is encrypted; CRL is not
OCSP provides real-time per-certificate status without downloading an entire revocation list
CRL requires a RADIUS server
OCSP is cheaper to implement
encounters.explanation: CRL (Certificate Revocation List) requires downloading the entire list of revoked certificates — slow and potentially stale (updated periodically). OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol) allows a client to query the revocation status of a single certificate in real time. Much more efficient.

encounters.question: PFS (Perfect Forward Secrecy) in IPsec/TLS ensures that:
options: The VPN never disconnects
If long-term keys are compromised, previously recorded encrypted sessions cannot be decrypted
All traffic is always encrypted with AES-256
Certificates are automatically renewed
encounters.explanation: PFS generates a unique ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key pair for each session. Even if the long-term private key is later compromised, past session recordings cannot be decrypted — each session used a different key that was never stored.

encounters.question: RSA is classified as which type of algorithm, and what is it primarily used for in TLS?
options: Symmetric — bulk encryption of session data
Asymmetric — key exchange and digital signatures (not bulk encryption)
Hashing — verifying data integrity
Block cipher — encrypting blocks of data
encounters.explanation: RSA is asymmetric (public/private key pair). In TLS it is used for key exchange (encrypting the pre-master secret) and digital signatures. It is NOT used for bulk data encryption — that's AES (symmetric, much faster). TLS uses RSA/ECDH to establish the session key, then AES for data.

encounters.question: IPsec AH (Authentication Header) provides which security service that ESP also provides?
options: Confidentiality (encryption)
Data origin authentication and integrity — but NOT encryption
NAT traversal support
Key management
encounters.explanation: AH (IP protocol 51) provides authentication and integrity only — it signs the entire IP packet but does NOT encrypt. ESP also provides authentication and integrity (plus encryption). The key difference: AH = no encryption; ESP = encryption. Use ESP.

encounters.question: A web browser displays a certificate error saying the certificate is not trusted. The most likely cause is:
options: The website is down
The certificate was not signed by a CA trusted in the browser's trust store (self-signed or unknown CA)
The TLS version is outdated
The website is using the wrong port
encounters.explanation: Browser trust is based on the certificate chain back to a trusted Root CA in the OS/browser trust store. If the certificate is self-signed or signed by an unknown CA (not in the trust store), the browser cannot verify authenticity and shows a trust error.

encounters.question: What IPsec ports/protocols must be permitted through a firewall for an IPsec VPN to function?
options: TCP 443 and TCP 1194
UDP 500 (IKE), UDP 4500 (NAT traversal), and IP protocol 50 (ESP)
TCP 1723 and GRE protocol 47
UDP 161 and UDP 162
encounters.explanation: IPsec requires: UDP 500 for IKE (key exchange/negotiation), UDP 4500 for NAT-T (NAT traversal — encapsulates ESP in UDP when NAT is present), and IP protocol 50 (ESP) for the actual encrypted data. If a firewall blocks these, the VPN fails.

encounters.question: GRE (Generic Routing Encapsulation) alone is insufficient for secure site-to-site tunnels. Why, and what is the solution?
options: GRE is too slow — use MPLS instead
GRE provides no encryption or authentication — combine with IPsec (GRE over IPsec) for security
GRE only supports IPv4 — use 6in4 instead
GRE cannot carry routing protocol updates
encounters.explanation: GRE (IP protocol 47) creates a tunnel that can carry any Layer 3 protocol including multicast/broadcast and routing protocol updates — but it is completely unencrypted and unauthenticated. GRE over IPsec = GRE tunnel wrapped in IPsec encryption for both flexibility and security.

nodes.name: The Gatehouse
nodes.description: AAA, RADIUS, TACACS+, 802.1X, NAC, port security, DHCP snooping, DAI, and ACLs.

encounters.title: Showing ID at the Door: 802.1X EAP Types
encounters.scenario: 802.1X can use different EAP methods — different ways of proving identity at a guarded door. With EAP-TLS, BOTH you and the guard show ID badges — mutual certificate authentication. Strongest option, but every visitor needs a badge issued in advance (a client cert from a PKI) — a heavy administrative lift. With PEAP, only the GUARD shows ID first (a server cert), creating a private encrypted booth; once inside, YOU prove identity the easy way — username and password (MSCHAPv2). No visitor badges needed, making PEAP far easier to roll out at scale. EAP-FAST is Cisco's lighter alternative, using a pre-shared 'Protected Access Credential' instead of a server cert. LEAP, Cisco's old method, skips the secure tunnel entirely and is crackable with offline tools — deprecated, never use it.
encounters.question: A company wants strong, certificate-based MUTUAL authentication for a small number of high-security lab devices, while a separate department wants to roll out 802.1X to thousands of BYOD laptops WITHOUT installing a client certificate on each one. Which EAP types fit these two needs, respectively?
options: EAP-FAST for the high-security devices; LEAP for the BYOD laptops

EAP-TLS for the high-security devices (mutual certificate auth — strongest available, but requires a client cert per device); PEAP for the BYOD laptops (server certificate builds an encrypted tunnel, then username/password authenticates inside it — no client cert needed)
LEAP for both, since it requires no certificates anywhere and works on any device
PEAP for the high-security devices (because it uses a tunnel) and EAP-TLS for the BYOD laptops (because it doesn't need a server certificate)
encounters.explanation: EAP-TLS needs a cert on BOTH client and server — strongest mutual auth, but requires a PKI to issue/distribute/revoke a cert per device, suiting a small pool of high-security endpoints. PEAP wraps username/password (MSCHAPv2) inside a TLS tunnel built from ONLY a server cert — clients need none, ideal for thousands of BYOD devices. Wrong: (A) EAP-FAST is roughly comparable to PEAP, not stronger than EAP-TLS, and LEAP is insecure everywhere. (C) LEAP's vulnerability to offline dictionary attacks rules it out entirely. (D) reverses the requirements — PEAP has no client cert, and EAP-TLS demands a server cert, the worst fit for 'no certificates at all.'

encounters.title: The Echo Chamber: Broadcast Storms and Storm Control
encounters.scenario: Picture two people each holding a megaphone pointed at each other — if one shouts, the other repeats it back, louder and louder, forever. This is a Layer 2 LOOP: if two switch ports connect to each other (directly or via a redundant path with no loop prevention), a broadcast frame gets forwarded back and forth endlessly, since Ethernet frames have NO TTL to expire. Within seconds this BROADCAST STORM consumes 100% of bandwidth and CPU on every switch in the loop. Spanning Tree Protocol normally PREVENTS loops by blocking redundant paths — but if STP is disabled or misconfigured, nothing stops it. STORM CONTROL is the safety net: a port feature that monitors what percentage of traffic is broadcast/multicast/unknown-unicast, and drops excess or err-disables the port once a threshold is exceeded.
encounters.question: A junior tech accidentally connects both ends of a spare patch cable into two access ports on the same switch. STP has been globally disabled on this switch for unrelated troubleshooting. Within seconds, every device on the switch loses connectivity and CPU utilization spikes to 100%. Which feature, if configured on those access ports, would have limited the damage even with STP disabled?
options: DHCP snooping — it would have blocked the looped traffic since it arrived on an untrusted port

Storm control — configured to monitor the percentage of broadcast traffic on each port and drop excess traffic or err-disable the port once a threshold is exceeded, capping the storm's impact regardless of why the loop exists
Port security — limiting MAC addresses per port would have stopped the broadcast storm, since loops generate excessive new MAC addresses
An extended ACL blocking broadcast traffic — ACLs are the standard mechanism switches use to limit broadcast storms
encounters.explanation: Storm control is a rate-based safety net for excessive broadcast/multicast/unknown-unicast traffic on a port — exactly the symptom of a Layer 2 loop, regardless of why it exists. It doesn't prevent the loop, but caps the damage. Wrong: (A) DHCP snooping filters DHCP messages and builds a binding table — unrelated to broadcast storms. (C) port security limits distinct MAC addresses per port; a storm is the SAME frame looping, not new MACs. (D) ACLs filter routed traffic by IP/port/protocol — not the rate-based Layer-2 tool for loop-induced storms.

encounters.question: RADIUS uses which transport protocol and ports for authentication?
options: TCP 49
UDP 1812 (auth) and UDP 1813 (accounting)
TCP 1812 and TCP 1813
UDP 514
encounters.explanation: RADIUS uses UDP 1812 for authentication/authorization and UDP 1813 for accounting. Legacy ports 1645/1646 also appear on exams. RADIUS uses UDP (connectionless) — compare with TACACS+ which uses TCP 49.

encounters.question: TACACS+ uses which protocol and port?
options: UDP 1812
TCP 49
UDP 162
TCP 443
encounters.explanation: TACACS+ (Terminal Access Controller Access Control System Plus) uses TCP port 49. TCP ensures reliable delivery — important for device administration sessions. It also encrypts the ENTIRE payload (unlike RADIUS which only encrypts the password).

encounters.question: In the 802.1X framework, what role does the network switch play?
options: Supplicant — provides credentials
Authenticator — forwards EAP between the client and RADIUS server
Authentication Server — verifies credentials
Certificate Authority — issues client certificates
encounters.explanation: 802.1X roles: Supplicant (client/endpoint providing credentials), Authenticator (switch or AP — forwards EAP messages between supplicant and RADIUS), Authentication Server (RADIUS — verifies credentials and returns Accept/Reject). The switch itself does not validate credentials.

encounters.question: The three components of AAA stand for:
options: Administration, Auditing, Accountability
Authentication, Authorisation, Accounting
Access, Authorisation, Auditing
Attestation, Authorisation, Accounting
encounters.explanation: AAA: Authentication (who are you? — verify identity), Authorisation (what can you do? — permissions/access rights), Accounting (what did you do? — logging for audit/billing). RADIUS and TACACS+ both provide AAA services.

encounters.question: Port security on a switch can be configured to allow only a specific number of MAC addresses per port. When a violation occurs, the default violation mode is:
options: Protect — silently drops frames from unknown MACs
Restrict — drops frames + sends SNMP alert
Shutdown — disables the port (err-disabled state)
Ignore — logs only, does not drop
encounters.explanation: The default port security violation mode is Shutdown — the port is placed in err-disabled state and must be manually re-enabled. Protect = silent drop. Restrict = drop + log/SNMP. Shutdown = port goes down (most disruptive but most obvious).

encounters.question: Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) relies on which other Layer 2 security feature to validate ARP packets?
options: Port security MAC table
DHCP snooping binding table
802.1X authentication state
IP Source Guard whitelist
encounters.explanation: DAI uses the DHCP snooping binding table — which maps MAC addresses to IP addresses based on legitimate DHCP transactions. When an ARP reply arrives on an untrusted port, DAI checks if the source MAC/IP pair matches the binding table. Mismatches = ARP poisoning → packet dropped.

encounters.question: A standard ACL vs an extended ACL: what additional matching criteria does an extended ACL provide?
options: VLAN membership
Destination IP, transport protocol (TCP/UDP), and source/destination port numbers
MAC address
ToS/DSCP values only
encounters.explanation: Standard ACL: matches source IP only (numbered 1–99). Extended ACL: matches source IP + destination IP + protocol (TCP/UDP/ICMP/etc.) + source/destination port numbers (numbered 100–199). Extended ACLs allow precise traffic control.

encounters.question: Extended ACLs should be placed as close to the SOURCE as possible. Why?
options: To reduce the number of ACL entries needed
To block traffic as early as possible — preventing unwanted traffic from traversing the network
To avoid affecting the destination router
Because extended ACLs only work at ingress interfaces near the source
encounters.explanation: Extended ACLs applied near the source drop unwanted traffic immediately — preventing it from wasting bandwidth traversing the network to be dropped later. Standard ACLs (source IP only) go near the destination to avoid over-blocking traffic from reaching other destinations.

encounters.question: RADIUS vs TACACS+: which encrypts the entire packet payload (not just the password)?
options: RADIUS — full packet encryption
TACACS+ — encrypts entire payload
Both encrypt the entire payload equally
Neither — both use plaintext
encounters.explanation: TACACS+ encrypts the entire packet body — credentials, authorisation data, accounting records. RADIUS only encrypts the password field in the Access-Request. This is why TACACS+ is preferred for device administration where commands are also logged.

encounters.question: NAC (Network Access Control) performs which function before granting network access?
options: Assigns VLANs based on SSID
Assesses endpoint posture (antivirus up-to-date, patches current, compliant with policy) before allowing access
Encrypts all traffic from the endpoint
Provides 802.1X RADIUS authentication only
encounters.explanation: NAC evaluates endpoint health/posture: is antivirus running and current? Are patches applied? Does it have a corporate certificate? Non-compliant endpoints are quarantined to a remediation VLAN where they can download updates, then re-assessed.

encounters.question: A user connects to a switch port with a new device. Port security with sticky MAC is enabled. What happens?
options: The port shuts down — sticky MAC only allows pre-configured MACs
The device's MAC is dynamically learned and saved to the running-config as the allowed MAC — only that device can use that port going forward
Any device is allowed — sticky MAC only logs MACs
The device must authenticate via 802.1X first
encounters.explanation: Sticky MAC: the first MAC address learned on the port is dynamically added to the port security configuration as the allowed MAC. If a different MAC tries to use that port, it triggers a violation. The sticky MAC is saved to running-config and persists across reboots if saved to startup-config.

encounters.question: Why is TACACS+ preferred over RADIUS for network device administration (managing routers/switches via CLI)?
options: TACACS+ supports more users
TACACS+ separates AAA services, encrypts the full payload, and supports per-command authorisation — critical for auditing admin CLI activity
RADIUS cannot authenticate network devices
TACACS+ is faster due to UDP transport
encounters.explanation: TACACS+ advantages for device admin: (1) full payload encryption — commands are private; (2) separated AAA — fine-grained per-command authorisation (restrict engineers to show commands only); (3) per-command accounting — complete audit trail of all CLI commands. RADIUS is better suited for network access auth (users connecting to Wi-Fi or VPN).

encounters.question: IP Source Guard on a switch port prevents:
options: ARP poisoning attacks
Hosts from sending traffic with a source IP address not assigned to them via DHCP
Rogue DHCP server attacks
MAC flooding attacks
encounters.explanation: IP Source Guard filters traffic on untrusted ports using the DHCP snooping binding table. Only packets with source IPs matching the binding table are forwarded. Hosts cannot spoof another host's IP address on the same segment.

encounters.question: DHCP snooping must be configured with trusted and untrusted ports. Which port should be marked as trusted?
options: All access ports connected to end users
The uplink port connecting to the legitimate DHCP server or core switch
Any port with a static IP configured
Only wireless AP ports
encounters.explanation: DHCP snooping trusted = ports that are allowed to send DHCP server messages (OFFER, ACK). Only uplink ports leading to the actual DHCP server should be trusted. All client-facing access ports are untrusted — DHCP OFFERs from those ports are dropped (prevents rogue DHCP).

encounters.question: An engineer configures a standard ACL to block traffic from 10.1.1.0/24 from reaching a file server at 192.168.10.5. Where should this ACL be applied?
options: On the router interface closest to the source (10.1.1.0/24 subnet)
On the router interface closest to the destination (192.168.10.5) — standard ACLs near destination
On the file server's NIC directly
On the core switch as a VACL
encounters.explanation: Standard ACLs match source IP only — if placed near the source, they would block traffic to ALL destinations from that subnet, not just the file server. Placed near the destination, they only block traffic headed to that specific interface/subnet. Always place standard ACLs close to the destination.

guardian_encounters.question: ARP poisoning is mitigated by which Layer 2 switch feature?
options: Port security
DHCP snooping
Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI)
Storm control
guardian_encounters.explanation: DAI validates ARP packets on untrusted ports against the DHCP snooping binding table. Invalid ARP replies (where MAC/IP doesn't match a known DHCP lease) are dropped — preventing ARP poisoning MITM attacks.

guardian_encounters.question: TACACS+ uses which transport protocol and port?
options: UDP 1812
UDP 1813
TCP 49
TCP 443
guardian_encounters.explanation: TACACS+ uses TCP 49. TCP ensures reliable delivery for device management sessions. RADIUS uses UDP 1812 (auth) / 1813 (accounting).

guardian_encounters.question: IPsec ESP (protocol 50) vs AH (protocol 51): which provides encryption?
options: AH provides encryption; ESP provides authentication only
ESP provides encryption + authentication; AH provides authentication only (no encryption)
Both provide encryption equally
Neither — they rely on GRE for encryption
guardian_encounters.explanation: ESP (IP protocol 50) = encryption + authentication + integrity. AH (IP protocol 51) = authentication + integrity ONLY — no encryption. In practice, always use ESP.

guardian_encounters.question: IDS vs IPS: which one can actively block malicious traffic?
options: IDS — detects and blocks
IPS — detects and blocks (inline)
Both can block equally
Neither — both only alert
guardian_encounters.explanation: IPS is deployed inline and can drop/block malicious traffic. IDS is passive (tap/SPAN mode) — detects and alerts only. IDS cannot block because traffic has already passed before detection.

guardian_encounters.question: Zero Trust security operates on which core principle?
options: Trust internal users; verify external users only
Never trust, always verify — all access requests require authentication regardless of network location
Trust is granted after initial MFA
Only cloud resources require Zero Trust
guardian_encounters.explanation: Zero Trust: no implicit trust — even inside the network perimeter. Every user and device must authenticate and be authorised for every resource, every time. Assumes breach has already occurred.

guardian_encounters.question: Password spraying avoids account lockout by:
options: Using a dictionary of complex passwords against one account
Trying a small number of common passwords across many accounts — staying under the per-account lockout threshold
Using GPU acceleration to try billions of passwords per second
Targeting only accounts with expired passwords
guardian_encounters.explanation: Spraying: try 'Password1' against 10,000 accounts — each account only sees 1 attempt (under lockout threshold). Brute force: try millions of passwords against 1 account — immediately triggers lockout. Spray = stealthy, slow, distributed.

guardian_encounters.question: A WAF (Web Application Firewall) specifically protects against:
options: Volumetric DDoS attacks
SQL injection, XSS, and other OWASP Top 10 web application attacks
ARP poisoning on the LAN
BGP route hijacking
guardian_encounters.explanation: WAF inspects HTTP/HTTPS application layer traffic for web-specific attacks (SQLi, XSS, CSRF, path traversal). Standard firewalls cannot detect these because they're embedded in legitimate-looking HTTP requests.

guardian_encounters.question: DHCP snooping must be configured before enabling DAI. Why?
options: DHCP snooping provides the certificate authority for DAI
DAI uses the DHCP snooping binding table (MAC-to-IP mappings) to validate ARP packets — without it, DAI has no reference data
DHCP snooping assigns VLAN membership used by DAI
DAI uses DHCP snooping port trust settings only
guardian_encounters.explanation: DAI validates ARP by checking the source MAC/IP against the DHCP snooping binding table. If DHCP snooping isn't running (no binding table), DAI cannot validate anything and will either pass or drop all traffic. DHCP snooping must populate the binding table first.

guardian_encounters.question: The implicit deny at the end of an ACL means:
options: The last explicit rule blocks all traffic
All traffic not matched by an explicit permit rule above is automatically dropped
Traffic is denied only on outbound interfaces
The deny applies to management traffic only
guardian_encounters.explanation: Every ACL has an invisible implicit deny all at the bottom. Any traffic reaching this rule (not matched above) is dropped silently. This is the most common cause of unexpected ACL blocking — forgetting to include a needed permit.

guardian_encounters.question: 802.1X port-based access: what state is the port in before authentication completes?
options: Authorised — all traffic permitted
Unauthorised — only EAP/802.1X traffic allowed; all other traffic blocked
Forwarding — same as standard switch port
Err-disabled — requires manual recovery
guardian_encounters.explanation: 802.1X port starts unauthorised — only EAPOL (EAP over LAN) authentication frames pass. No IP traffic permitted until RADIUS returns Access-Accept. Then the port moves to authorised state. Guest VLAN can be configured for devices that fail 802.1X.

guardian_encounters.question: DNS poisoning is best mitigated by:
options: Enabling HTTPS-only on web servers
DNSSEC — cryptographically signs DNS responses so forged records are detected and rejected
Increasing DNS TTL values
Using RADIUS for DNS authentication
guardian_encounters.explanation: DNSSEC adds cryptographic signatures to DNS records. Resolvers verify the signature chain — forged or modified DNS responses fail signature validation and are rejected. Also: use encrypted DNS (DoH/DoT) to prevent interception.

guardian_encounters.question: RADIUS encrypts only the password in authentication packets. TACACS+ encrypts:
options: Only the username
The entire packet payload
Only accounting records
Nothing — TACACS+ uses TLS externally
guardian_encounters.explanation: TACACS+ encrypts the entire body of every packet — credentials, commands, authorization, accounting data. RADIUS only encrypts the password field. This makes TACACS+ more secure for device management where command history is sensitive.

guardian_encounters.question: PFS (Perfect Forward Secrecy) protects against which specific threat?
options: Brute force of current session keys
Decryption of previously recorded traffic if long-term private keys are later compromised
Certificate revocation failures
Replay attacks
guardian_encounters.explanation: Without PFS, an attacker who records encrypted traffic and later obtains the server's private key can decrypt all past sessions. PFS generates a unique ephemeral key per session (Diffie-Hellman) — past sessions remain protected even if the long-term key is compromised.

guardian_encounters.question: A DMZ (screened subnet) in a two-firewall design restricts traffic how?
options: Internet → DMZ allowed. DMZ → internal LAN blocked by inner firewall. Internal → DMZ allowed.
Internet → DMZ blocked. DMZ → internal LAN allowed.
All traffic between all zones is blocked by default.
DMZ and internal LAN are the same security zone.
guardian_encounters.explanation: Two-firewall DMZ: outer firewall allows internet to reach DMZ servers (web, mail, DNS). Inner firewall blocks DMZ from initiating connections to the internal LAN. Internal users can reach DMZ. A compromised DMZ server cannot reach internal systems.

guardian_encounters.question: Whaling is a specific type of spear phishing that targets:
options: Maritime organisations
Senior executives and C-suite (CEO, CFO, COO)
Network administrators specifically
Employees with database access
guardian_encounters.explanation: Whaling = 'going after the big fish' — highly targeted spear phishing against senior executives. Attackers research the target thoroughly. Common themes: fake legal subpoenas, wire transfer requests (BEC — Business Email Compromise), regulatory notices.

guardian_encounters.question: A standard ACL should be placed close to the DESTINATION. An extended ACL should be placed close to the SOURCE. Why the difference?
options: Standard ACLs are more complex and require more processing near the destination

Standard ACLs only match source IP — placing near source would block all traffic from that source to ALL destinations. Near destination = only blocks traffic to that specific destination. Extended ACLs match src+dst so can safely filter near source.
Extended ACLs use more memory and need to be near the source to conserve resources
There is no difference — both should be placed near the source
guardian_encounters.explanation: Standard ACL near source = blocks ALL traffic from that source to everywhere (too broad). Near destination = only affects traffic going to that specific subnet. Extended ACL near source = precise enough (knows src+dst+port) to block only intended traffic, and kills it early before it wastes bandwidth.

guardian_encounters.question: An evil twin AP differs from a rogue AP in that:
options: Evil twin uses stronger encryption than the legitimate AP
Evil twin broadcasts the same SSID as the legitimate AP to trick users into connecting — enabling MITM
Rogue AP is set up outside the building; evil twin is inside
They are the same thing
guardian_encounters.explanation: Rogue AP: any unauthorised AP connected to the corporate network. Evil twin: a rogue AP that mimics a legitimate AP's SSID to deceive users — it may not even be connected to the corporate network. Users connect thinking it's real; attacker intercepts traffic.

guardian_encounters.question: A SYN flood is a Protocol DDoS attack. What mechanism does it exploit, and what is the primary mitigation?
options: It exploits DNS cache — mitigated by DNSSEC
It exploits TCP 3-way handshake — sends many SYN packets but never completes handshake, exhausting server state tables. Mitigated by SYN cookies.
It exploits ICMP echo — mitigated by blocking ICMP
It exploits BGP — mitigated by route filtering
guardian_encounters.explanation: SYN flood fills the server's half-open connection table — server reserves resources for each SYN waiting for the final ACK that never comes. SYN cookies: server encodes session state in the SYN-ACK sequence number — no state allocated until ACK received with valid cookie.

guardian_encounters.question: Defense in depth differs from Zero Trust in that defense in depth:
options: Replaces perimeter security with identity-based access
Layers multiple overlapping security controls — perimeter, internal, host, data — so one failure doesn't mean full compromise
Assumes breach has already occurred
Eliminates trust for all internal traffic
guardian_encounters.explanation: Defense in depth = multiple security layers (network, host, application, data). Zero Trust = authentication/authorisation model: no implicit trust regardless of location, continuous verification. They are complementary — Zero Trust is a subset principle that fits within defense in depth.

guardian_encounters.question: IPsec tunnel mode vs transport mode — which is used for remote access VPN (laptop → corporate HQ)?
options: Transport mode — encrypts payload only, IP header preserved
Tunnel mode — encrypts entire original packet with new outer IP header
Both modes work equally for remote access
Neither — remote access VPN uses GRE only
guardian_encounters.explanation: Remote access VPN (laptop → corporate HQ) typically uses tunnel mode — the client's private IP is encapsulated inside the VPN tunnel with a new outer IP header containing the client's public IP and VPN gateway IP. The original private-addressed packet is fully encrypted inside.
